notes: A football index per country and year (→ECON-26): what football itself pays and charges, beyond consumer prices. Every figure here is our own estimate derived from published aggregates, never a reproduced national revenue series, so each era is labelled estimated (→ECON-3); years after the coverage year are projected like prices (→ECON-2).

The index is the country's price index multiplied by a real multiple normalised to the base year (1950 = 1). England's multiple is about 1 until 1979, 2 by 1992, 6 by 2005, 10 by 2020 and 11 by 2025; every other country reaches the share of England's real growth recorded as its share, so real = 1 + share × (England's real − 1). Within an era the multiple grows geometrically from the previous anchor; the first era is flat, so the index tracks prices until commercialisation.

Sponsor-slot opening years (→ECON-8) record the year a slot first existed in a country's football: local partners in every era, then the kit supplier, the shirt front, stadium naming and the sleeve. England's years are 1970, 1979, 1997 and 2017. A year that rests on an era rather than on a documented first is labelled estimated.

notes: A broadcasting index per country and year (→ECON-31): what a league's central money, above all its television rights, is worth beyond consumer prices; league distributions (→ECON-28) are quoted on it instead of the football index. Every figure is our own estimate from the published history of league rights deals, never a reproduced national revenue series, so each era is labelled estimated (→ECON-3); after the coverage year the last real multiple holds and prices are projected (→ECON-2).

The index is the country's price index multiplied by a real multiple against prices, on the football index's footing (1 = prices, as the football index is at its 1950 base) but well below 1 before television sold league football. England's multiple is 0.15 until 1950, 0.3 by 1964 (regular league highlights on television), 1 by 1983 (the first live league contracts), 6 by 1992 (pay-television and the Premier League), 25 by 2005, 45 by 2020 and 48 by 2025. Within an era the multiple grows geometrically from the previous anchor; the first era is flat.

Every other country's multiple is 0.15 plus its football-index share of England's growth above 0.15, rounded to two decimals. Spain, Germany, Italy, Portugal, the Netherlands and Belgium reached pay-television's large league contracts after England, so at 1992 they hold their share of England's 1988 multiple; France, whose league Canal+ has shown live since 1984, follows England's path.
